title: Philippine Immigration Detention: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer held for 41 days in the Philippines saw not a prison but a business with prices posted on everything: a bed, a boxed meal, a phone, a lawyer's fee. Those who don't pay stay for years, sometimes more than a decade.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series — medium information density but solid detail. The first half is one man's ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers who raise their price on the spot — is where the real value is.
who: Founders and overseas-expansion operators interested in the situation of Chinese abroad, the Philippine business environment, and the mechanics of gray industry and immigration corruption.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — the surfing career and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: The Immigration Bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, an immigration officer pulled him aside and said quietly, "I can help you." After the lawyer communicated with them, the answer came back: give 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can be released immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 or 13 people arrested in the same batch, no one agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing still existed in 2026 and wanted to resolve it through normal legal procedure. But the price of refusing was this: they were transferred from the holding cells of the General Santos police station to the Immigration Bureau detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When the phone was taken, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was confiscated, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was normal procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — Gcash being the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied repeatedly and could not get the phone back, until he kept pressing the Chinese consulate and his lawyer, and it was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — then transferred back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in it. Feili says it isn't about the amount; it's that the phone was touched while it wasn't in his hands. His read: many Chinese in Manila working in gray-industry scams go through this same shakedown after arrest, but they don't dare approach the Chinese consulate, because their phones hold a mass of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the Immigration Bureau promised exist — in another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket for the transfer, the Immigration Bureau works on them in shifts, saying conditions at the Manila bureau are excellent: air conditioning, plenty of freedom, a gym, basketball, takeout delivery, phone use. Feili says they weren't lying — there really is air conditioning, you really can order takeout, it's just another form, a completely different form. They arrived at the main bureau's detention center after 3 a.m. What he saw getting out of the vehicle was a square compound: an outer layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof above, iron cages like dog kennels on all sides, and inside them long communal platforms holding several hundred people. At past 3 a.m. many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, they clung to the cage bars to stare at the newcomers. Feili says he and the other foreigners said nothing for several minutes after getting out, then it hit them: the Immigration Bureau had lied to them.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this Immigration Bureau detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss in cooperation with the bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by that Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese who came in had to pay. The cheapest tier, a spot on the communal platform, was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy pan zong and gambling bosses could pay 50,000 pesos a month, over 6,000 RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — in fact the bed was the same, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bed. That is where the Immigration Bureau's earlier promise of "air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were their investment and there was no way to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, that he was here to serve time — how could he be expected to pay as well? The gang boss said in a threatening tone: you're already in here, you don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run through gang divisions, with the Chinese gang monopolizing all food, clothing and daily life for Chinese inmates, operating a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center held about 200 people; when Feili arrived it was the low season and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them from gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's staff draw wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the kitchen helper 5,000 pesos. The pay is very low, but many people can't get out precisely because they have no money for a lawyer, so they can only work to earn.

points.h: A man from Yunnan held over a year; his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he had been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken and he was dragged into a compound to run telecom fraud, and when his numbers were poor his supervisor shocked him with a stun baton every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the Immigration Bureau detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own ticket, and you leave — but the Immigration Bureau, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time, and without paying the procedure doesn't move. He had already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese and translate it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden, who had a guard bring Feili's phone so the young man could add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterwards the Immigration Bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese person Feili talked with at any length came from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people had been surrounded by three agencies — the Immigration Bureau together with the police and the NBI. The first shakedown was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet, because there are no cameras in the toilets, and stripping them of everything valuable. The second was the Immigration Bureau negotiating ransoms with the company boss — the quote differed per person, 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos, depending on the negotiator's mood. That company's deal was 3 million pesos per person, over 300,000 RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; in his best month he took in 2 million RMB, and bought a house and a car in his small home county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, several hundred thousand was transferred out, and a corrupt cop pinned an illegal gun-possession charge on him, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: A Philippine lawyer raises the price the moment he sees you're Chinese
points.body: In Cebu, Feili was introduced by a Lithuanian to a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, over 20,000 RMB, to settle it in four weeks. After Feili reached Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and raised the price on the spot, saying the earlier figure was the old price and the new price required another 120,000 pesos, over 10,000 RMB. Feili decided not to use him and abandoned the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted over 30,000 RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili says the genuinely reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedural pipeline extremely well, because everyone locked up inside is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, 41 days counting Cebu. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili messaged him.

Look at his corrupt bureaucratic system and its people as separate things. I still believe Filipinos are by nature very good people. But the bureaucratic system is truly too corrupt — and it drinks blood, the kind of bureaucratic system that drinks human blood.
